questions.q: What is a purely reactive SOC's real limitation?
options: Anything that doesn't trigger an existing correlation rule goes completely unnoticed, no matter how long it's happening
It can never respond to any alert at all
It is always more expensive to run than a proactive SOC
It only works during business hours by definition
questions.explain: A reactive SOC is purely alert-driven, so nothing without a matching rule ever surfaces for review.

questions.q: In the slow-exfiltration example, why would a purely reactive SOC never notice it?
options: The traffic stays under every threshold a correlation rule checks for, so no rule ever fires and nothing is ever reviewed
The SOC has no logging enabled at all
Exfiltration traffic is always encrypted and therefore invisible
The SOC's firewall actively blocks all outbound traffic
questions.explain: Nothing crosses a threshold, so nothing fires — and a reactive SOC only looks at what fires.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three proactive practices described in this lesson?
options: Threat hunting: deliberately searching data for signs of compromise that existing rules wouldn't catch
Disabling all correlation rules entirely
Only reviewing alerts once a year
Refusing to track any SOC metrics at all
questions.explain: Threat hunting is the practice that surfaces exactly what a reactive, alert-only SOC would otherwise miss.

questions.q: What do MTTD and MTTR measure, and why does a maturing SOC track them?
options: Mean time to detect and mean time to respond — tracked so the SOC knows objectively whether it's actually improving
The number of analysts employed and their average salary
The total dollar cost of the SOC's software licenses
How many coffee breaks analysts take per shift
questions.explain: MTTD and MTTR give a SOC an objective, metrics-driven way to confirm real improvement instead of assuming it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does a SOC actually move from reactive toward proactive?
options: Proactive practices get layered on top of the reactive baseline over time as staffing, tooling, and experience grow
It flips instantly the moment leadership approves a budget increase
It happens automatically once a SIEM is purchased
A SOC is either reactive or proactive from the day it's founded, and never changes
questions.explain: Maturity is layered, not a single flip — most real SOCs sit somewhere in between for a long time.
